The etiological framework, specifically the selected-effect account, provides the only adequate foundation for biological function because it successfully accounts for the inherent normativity of functional language, including the crucial concept of malfunction. According to the selected-effect view, the function of a biological trait is defined by the specific effect for which that trait was favored by natural selection in ancestral organisms. This historical grounding establishes an objective normative standard of what the trait is supposed to do, regardless of its current physical state or performance. By tying function to evolutionary history, the etiological account explains how a trait can fail to perform its function. For instance, a malformed or diseased heart that is incapable of pumping blood still possesses the function of pumping blood, because it is a member of a trait-kind that was selected for that specific effect. A purely dispositional or causal-role analysis, which defines function solely in terms of current causal contributions, cannot accommodate this distinction. If function is merely a current disposition, then a heart that cannot pump blood simply lacks the disposition to do so, meaning its failure to pump cannot be classified as a malfunction; it is merely behaving according to its current physical state. Thus, only the etiological account preserves the normative distinction between what a trait actually does and what it is biologically supposed to do.

Furthermore, causal-role accounts, such as those modeled after Robert Cummins, are fundamentally incapable of distinguishing a trait’s genuine biological functions from its mere accidental effects without surrendering the objectivity of functional attribution. In a Cummins-style analysis, a function is identified as any causal contribution a component makes to a larger capacity of a containing system. Without the historical constraint of natural selection, however, there is no principled, mind-independent way to separate a trait's evolutionary purpose from its coincidental side effects. For example, the heart contributes to the capacity of the body to circulate blood, but it also contributes to the capacity of medical professionals to hear heartbeats through a stethoscope. Under a purely causal-role view, both of these contributions count as functions unless one artificially privileges certain system capacities over others. To make this distinction, causal-role theorists must relativize functional attributions to the specific explanatory interests of the investigator. Consequently, whether a trait has a function, and what that function is, becomes a subjective matter dependent on the cognitive goals of the scientist rather than an objective, mind-independent fact about the organism itself. The etiological account avoids this relativism by grounding functions in the objective, historical process of natural selection, ensuring that functional claims remain discoveries about nature rather than inventions of the observer.

Finally, etiological accounts alone vindicate the unique explanatory force of functional claims in biological science by answering the fundamental question of why a trait is present in an organism. When biologists assert that the function of the kidney is to filter blood, they are not merely offering a mechanical description of what the kidney currently does; they are providing a teleological explanation for why kidneys exist in the organismal population. The etiological account directly addresses this historical question by showing that the current presence of the trait is a causal consequence of past selection for that very effect; kidneys exist today because ancestral kidneys filtered blood, thereby enhancing the fitness of those ancestors. In contrast, causal-role accounts are restricted to describing the current, synchronic operations of a system, answering the question of how a mechanism currently operates rather than why it exists. Citing a trait's current causal role cannot explain why the organism possesses that trait in the first place, as a current effect cannot causally explain its own pre-existing structural cause. By linking function to the selective history that brought the trait into being, the etiological account provides a robustly explanatory framework that justifies why functional language is indispensable to evolutionary biology.
